UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interim Resource Adequacy 
Service and Large Load Registry 
)  
)            Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
) 
PROTEST OF PJM POWER PROVIDERS GROUP 
PJM is at a critical moment in its history. Facing the challenges presented 
by the emergence of potentially significant new large demand and finding the 
market-based means of building the capacity to support the new growth will 
demand economically rational and structurally sound market design.  Now is 
precisely the time that PJM and the Commission need to dedicate themselves to 
the proposition that a properly designed and well-functioning market will ultimately 
serve the consumers of the PJM region by providing reliability at the least cost. 
Unfortunately, the interim resource adequacy service (“IRAS”)1 and large 
load registry proposal (the “IRAS Proposal”) PJM has submitted represents an ill-
conceived and unnecessary step away from PJM’s core principles and, perhaps 
more troubling, has long term implications for PJM’s capacity construct that may 
permanently scar it.  PJM’s IRAS Proposal reflects an untested and unsupported, 
unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory experiment with the nation’s 
largest power grid that has historically provided the consumers of the region with 
reliable service at competitive capacity prices.  Astoundingly, PJM asks the 
 
1 PJM’s nomenclature of “interim” in the context of IRAS is misleading.  PJM does not 
propose that the program sunset, but rather it is filed as a permanent program.

2 
Commission to sanction this experiment with not as much as a single economist’s 
or market design witness’ testimony, analysis, study or supporting data.    
The PJM Power Providers Group (“P3”)2 recognizes the pressure on the 
Commission and PJM to implement reforms to address the unprecedented load 
growth associated with New Large Loads and the potential price impact thereof on 
consumers. 3  Unfortunately, however, the IRAS Proposal represents an 
abandonment of core tenets of the PJM capacity construct that will provide 
troubling messages to both new and existing capacity resources, jeopardizing 
reliability and resource adequacy, while raising the specter of litigation that is 
bound to interject further uncertainty at the very moment that certainty is 
paramount.     
The IRAS Proposal cannot and should not be approved in accordance with 
Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) as it is unjust, unreasonable and 
unduly discriminatory and preferential and will increase costs and undermine 
regional resource adequacy.4  For one, it explicitly is premised on the imposition 
of discriminatory treatment of certain classes of generators and certain types of 
customers, and the discrimination it proposes is undue. And second, PJM is

leagues away from having met its burden of proof to support the proposal.  Third, 
the IRAS Proposal is facially inconsistent with both FPA Sections 2015 and 215,6 
and also cannot be approved on that basis.   
On the merits of a review of the soundness of IRAS as a market-design 
proposal, the IRAS Proposal must be rejected for a plethora of reasons, including: 
 Put simply, IRAS sends the wrong incentives.  It reflects bad market 
design policy, and impermissibly deviates from well-established 
precedent, because PJM seeks to remedy recently-experienced 
shortfalls in its Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) capacity 
procurement, counterintuitively, by artificially suppressing the price 
signals that are needed to incentivize the capacity PJM needs to 
remain in and enter into the market in order to cure the resource 
adequacy shortfall; 
 It proposes to reduce reliability by intentionally under-procuring 
capacity. It is unsupported by evidence to warrant its fundamental 
restructuring of the RPM demand curve it proposes, given that the 
only filed affidavit – by Christopher Pilong – focused only on 
operations, not market analysis, price impacts, or loss-of-load 
expectation analysis. Specifically, there is no analysis of either the 
short or long-term implications of acting as if load that actually exists 
does not exist in the RPM process;   
 IRAS dangerously degrades the regional reliability standard by 
treating IRAS as akin to accredited capacity when it is not, effectively 
changing the regional reliability criteria in the process, again without 
providing any support, let alone acknowledgment, of that effect and 
without addressing the consequences of such change.  IRAS is an 
involuntary reduction of service and represents a degradation of 
reliability;   
 IRAS is impermissibly vague as a rate filing because it depends on 
the outcome of state retail proceedings that may or may not ever 
occur and PJM cannot compel; and 
 IRAS is an untested and unsupported experiment that seeks to 
inappropriately commandeer North American Electric Reliability 
Corporation (“NERC”) Reliability Standards that apply to the Bulk 
Electric System for use on the retail distribution system for which they 
 
5 16 U.S.C. § 824. 
6 16 U.S.C. § 824o.

4 
were not designed, representing another way the proposal puts 
reliability at risk.  
 If approved, the IRAS filing will have long-lasting implications for 
PJM’s capacity construct, resource adequacy and costs that will not 
easily be rectified.  Load on PJM’s system will be eliminated from the 
Variable Resource Requirement (“VRR”) Curve with no firm 
enforcement mechanism governing the satisfaction of that load’s 
demand. This departs from the checks and balances associated with 
every other type of load reduction, which each are paired with 
enforceable obligations (e.g., Fixed Resource Requirement (“FRR”), 
Demand Resources, Price Responsive Demand, Peak Shaving 
Adjustments and behind-the-meter generation).  This reduction of 
load unpaired with an enforceable obligation to procure sufficient 
capacity to meet the demand represents an incredibly dangerous 
and perhaps irreversible policy divergence from one of the PJM 
capacity market’s core tenets.    
I. 
PROTEST 
A. 
The Federal Power Act Dictates Rejection of the IRAS Proposal 
1. 
PJM Has Not Met Its Burden of Proof  
Under FPA Section 205, the filing public utility proposing tariff revisions 
bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that its proposal is just, reasonable, and 
not unduly discriminatory or preferential.7  It is not the Commission’s role to resolve 
the evidentiary gaps in order to develop the substantial evidence that would be 
required to accept a proposal that was inadequately supported when filed. 8  
 
7 16 U.S.C. § 824d. 
8 See Sw. Power Pool, Inc. GridLiance High Plains LLC, 180 FERC ¶ 61,192 at P 52 (2022) 
(“The party with the burden of proof bears the burden of production, or the need to provide 
sufficient evidence to establish a prima facie case”); see also, e.g., Nantahala Power & 
Light Co. v. FERC, 727 F.2d 1342, 1351 (4th Cir. 1984) (“Nantahala”) (“A utility bears the 
burden of justifying each component of” a proposed rate change and “[b]ecause a regulated 
utility is the party with access to the necessary information, it bears the risk of an 
undeveloped or inconclusive record”); Nw. Corp. v. FERC, 884 F.3d 1176, 1182-83 (D.C. 
Cir. 2018) (explaining that “because it was [the utility’s] burden under Section 205 to show 
that its proposed rate was just and reasonable, [] failure [to do so] was fatal” and rejecting 
arguments that it was FERC’s burden to identify alternative bases for finding the proposed 
rate just and reasonable); Advanced Energy Mgmt. All. v. FERC, 860 F.3d 656, 662 (D.C. 
Cir. 2017) (explaining, in the context of the Section 205 burden of proof, that “[w]hen acting

5 
Rather, the Commission routinely rejects Section 205 filings when the filing utility  
fails to meet its burden of proof,9  and it is most critical that it do so here, because 
of the substantial and fundamental negative consequences and market design 
flaws endemic to the IRAS Proposal.  As described herein, PJM has not come 
close to satisfying this burden and, as such, the Commission should reject the 
IRAS proposal for that reason alone. 
Notably, PJM relies on a single affidavit as the evidentiary support for its 
entire ground-breaking IRAS Proposal: the affidavit of Christopher Pilong, its 
Senior Director of Operations Planning.10  That affidavit addresses only operational 
issues, including emergency procedures and dispatch sequencing.11  At the IRAS 
Proposal’s peril,12 and confoundingly given the import of the proposal, PJM opted 
 
on a public utility’s rate filing under section 205, the Commission undertakes ‘an essentially 
passive and reactive role’ and restricts itself to evaluating the confined proposal”). 
9 Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 191 FERC ¶ 61,131 at P 197 (2025) 
(rejecting tariff revisions where filer failed to meet Section 205 burden show approach for 
addressing resource adequacy and reliability needs was just and reasonable and not 
unduly discriminatory or preferential); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 180 FERC ¶ 61,089 at 
PP 47, 51 (2022) (rejecting PJM tariff revisions because PJM failed to meet Section 205 
burden to show proposal was just and reasonable), order on reh’g, 181 FERC ¶ 61,191 at 
P 15 n.49 (2022) (stating “PJM bears the burden of proof to show that the . . . proposal is 
just and reasonable”) (citing 16 U.S.C. § 824d(e); Nw. Corp. v. FERC, 884 F.3d 1176, 1182 
(D.C. Cir. 2018); Panda Stonewall LLC, Opinion No. 574, 174 FERC ¶ 61,266 at P 30 
(2021)); PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 168 FERC ¶ 61,133 at P 25 (2019) (rejecting filing 
where Section 205 burden was not met).

Interconnection, L.L.C. (“Pilong Aff.”).

As a consequence, among other things, PJM failed to quantify the clearing-price 
effect on costs and resource adequacy of excluding New Large Loads that do not 
Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) from the VRR curve, provided no 
analysis of the resource adequacy or cost effect of the decade of mandated 
$0/MW-Day offers its proposal would impose, omitted a loss-of-load-expectation 
study or any explanation as to the effect its proposal would have on its long-held 
and widely accepted loss-of-load expectations and whether any change thereof is 
just or reasonable, and neglected to estimate the MW volumes that would be 
excluded from the VRR curve. 
While PJM’s burden to carry would not differ if its IRAS Proposal had 
substantial stakeholder support, PJM’s omissions of evidentiary support as to 
market design, economic merit and reliability are even more glaring given that the 
IRAS Proposal in fact did not have widespread stakeholder support, as PJM 
concedes that all of the “proposals regarding the concepts addressed by IRAS 
failed to achieve two-thirds stakeholder support.”13

must hold PJM to meeting, Attachment DD, Section 5.10(a)(iii) of PJM's Tariff 
requires that any review of the VRR Curve be grounded in simulations of market 
conditions establishing, on a probabilistic basis, that the curve will procure

support its orders accepting these VRR Curve adjustments.16  Here,  in contrast to 
its actions in the periodic review, PJM proposes to alter the quantity on which every

and other evidence filed by PJM.  Here, in contrast, where the consequences of the change 
are in a whole other league to the tiny 1.5% curve shift proposed in the sixth quadrennial

in its proposal.

point of the VRR Curve is anchored, a change that bears on procurement 
adequacy at least as directly as a change in the curve's slope, while submitting no 
simulation, no probabilistic analysis, no loss-of-load-expectation study (or even 
consideration of loss-of-load impacts), no sensitivity analysis, no related 
independent expert testimony, and no estimate of the MW quantity that will be 
excluded for the Base Residual Auction (“BRA”) by the IRAS Proposal.  PJM does 
not explain why a modification of this consequence warrants less analytical support 
than its Tariff demands for a modification of the curve's shape in a quadrennial 
review, and the Commission would be shirking its regulatory responsibilities were 
it to  accept such consequential changes without the important data such modeling 
and analysis would provide, especially in the face of meaningful evidence that the 
IRAS Proposal, if implemented, would exacerbate resource adequacy issues in 
PJM and result in increased costs overall.  The Commission cannot accept this 
filing without departing from the standards, and rigorous evidence requirements, it 
just recently required to justify a change to the VRR Curve and departing from 
troves of well-established precedent. 
2. 
The Commission Cannot Cure the Defects in the IRAS 
Proposal by Accepting It Subject to Condition; Rejection 
is its Only Option. 
In an acknowledgement of the controversy surrounding its IRAS Proposal, 
PJM preemptively provided notice in the filing that it would consent to the 
Commission’s use of authority to modify or sever portions of the proposed Open 
Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement (“RAA”)

9 
changes in the proposal, if deemed necessary and appropriate under FPA Section 
205 and if consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives.17 
The Commission cannot condition acceptance on modifications to the IRAS 
Proposal, however, as FPA Section 205 limits the Commission to a “passive and 
reactive role” 18  and the relevant precedents disallow modifications to a filed 
proposal where the modification would transform the proposal into an entirely 
different rate design.19 The defects requiring correction in the IRAS Proposal are 
substantial and pervasive and would run afoul of the permitted “minor” 
modifications precedents permit. Moreover, the consent to Commission alterations 
that PJM granted in the filing itself is extremely circumscribed and insufficient to 
allow the proposal’s major defects to be cured.20 
In NRG, the Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit acted on a PJM Section 
205 capacity market filing in a situation similar to the one the Commission confronts 
here. PJM had filed a package of revisions to the Minimum Offer Price Rule, parts

Commission proposed modifications it believed would cure the deficiency, and 
accepted the filing as so modified, obtaining PJM’s consent.21 The D.C. Circuit 
nonetheless vacated, holding that “Section 205 does not allow FERC to make 
modifications to a proposal that transform the proposal into an entirely new rate of 
FERC’s own making,” and that the Commission’s modifications had produced an

Here, as discussed further infra, rehabilitating the PJM rate proposal would 
require, inter alia, removing PJM’s proposed exclusion of load from the VRR Curve, 
excluding the ten-year price taker mandate, and allowing existing capacity to 
compete on equal footing to new capacity in PJM’s BYONC scheme.  Fundamental 
changes of such magnitude would neither be consistent with the Commission’s 
reactionary role under NRG, nor fall within the circumscribed consent to changes 
PJM provided.

B. 
PJM’s Proposal Would Inappropriately Stifle Supply from 
Responding to the Resource Adequacy Challenge 
1. 
For the VRR Curve Development Only, PJM Improperly 
Will Treat Load on the System as if it Doesn’t Exist 
Starting as of the 2029/2030 Delivery Year, PJM proposes to remove from 
both the Regional Transmission Organization (“RTO”)-wide and Locational 
Deliverability Area (“LDA”) VRR Curves the unforced capacity (“UCAP”) of New 
Large Loads that do not BYONC or procure capacity in its newly-proposed and 
not-yet-approved Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) auction, measured 
against the 2028/2029 BRA load forecast.24  In other words, PJM seeks to erase 
load from the demand curve notwithstanding that the load actually exists on the 
system.  PJM understands the load is actually on the system, and has not 
proposed that the required transmission or other required infrastructure need not 
be built to reliably serve this load, just that the load will not be included in the 
demand curve. Removing forecasted load from the quantity procured moves the 
Demand Curve to the left. Once the auction clears on a price-responsive segment, 
that reduction lowers the clearing price, which signals to existing supply that it 
should exit and to new supply that it should not invest.   
As P3 Witness Carl Coscia concludes in the attached affidavit, PJM’s IRAS 
Proposal is inconsistent with the design of RPM, which was developed to deliver 
the Net Cost of New Entry as revenue to a capacity resource on average over the 
asset’s life in capacity revenue to supplement the revenues provided by the energy 
 
24 PJM Transmittal Letter at 109-114; proposed Tariff, Definitions – Excluded RTO New 
Large Load Amounts and Excluded LDA New Large Load Amounts.

12 
and ancillary services markets.25  RPM was to provide the missing money to attract 
and retain needed resources, yet PJM has not shown that the IRAS Proposal will 
not exacerbate the missing money problem.  Mr. Coscia provides analysis 
indicating that clearing prices below the Net Cost of New Entry across successive 
Delivery Years are outcomes of this model change.26  He indicates that RPM was 
adopted in the first place due to “a spike in announced retirements of units that 
nonetheless are needed for reliability,” and considering PJM’s warning that 
“generator revenues in PJM may not be adequate to sustain the investments 
needed to maintain reliability in all parts of the PJM region.”27 
Notwithstanding PJM’s historical experience and the Commission’s 
response acknowledging the importance of permitting an opportunity to recover 
the Net Cost of New Entry over time, Mr. Coscia concludes as follows: 
If the filing is accepted, PJM will construct the 2029/2030 Demand 
Curve using the reduced procurement base. The reduction will recur 
as qualifying load enters the forecast and will apply whether or not 
PJM ultimately calls an Interim Resource Adequacy Service event. 
Under the scenarios examined, the immediate effect is a smaller 
procurement target and increased sensitivity to the location of supply 
relative to Point 1; after the collar expires, several modeled paths 
produce materially lower clearing prices than the most recent Net 
Cost of New Entry calculation published by PJM.28

2. 
PJM’s VRR Curve Reset Will Cause Fewer Resources to 
Clear Despite its Need For Additional Resources to Meet 
Increasing Demand, Increasing Shortages and Leading to 
Increased Prices. 
Mr. Coscia models the effect of the load exclusion subsumed in the IRAS 
Proposal on RPM clearing prices, showing that the capacity market clearing prices 
with the demand exclusion begin a downward trajectory, quickly leading to a >50% 
reduction in the clearing price by 2030/2031 in the modeled scenario regardless of 
PJM’s projected continuing needs for additional capacity (e.g., the modeled clearing 
price falls from the Point 1 price of $554.72/MW-day to $206.02/MW-day in 
2030/2031 and to $156.79/MW-day by 2032/2033):29   
 
 
Thus, while PJM has represented that it is entering the 2027/2028 Delivery 
Year short of capacity because load is growing faster than supply,30 its solution 
counter-intuitively is to exacerbate the shortage it states it is seeking to remedy.  
At the same time, PJM has not provided, and cannot provide, evidence that the 
Cost of New Entry or the return on investment that investors require has

decreased. Thus, despite PJM having more load than it can serve reliably, the 
RPM auction post-IRAS would send the improper signal that existing resources 
whose offers exceed those depressed clearing prices and that therefore do not 
clear should exit the market.  Similarly, the message will be sent that new 
resources that cannot be financially sustained at the depressed clearing prices 
should stay out, and resource adequacy will continue to suffer in the region.  As a 
result of this effect on the RPM market, reliable service in PJM — even service to 
the “existing” load — will be degraded.  This will force PJM to again engage in one 
or more out-of-market stop-gap measures to shore up resource adequacy for even 
adequate service to existing load, but as with its other out-of-market measures, the 
solutions will not be as efficient as those driven by the market and ultimately will 
be more costly for consumers in PJM.31

just because it may yield lower RPM BRA clearing prices.  The feedback loop is

growth increases the system PJM must plan to serve; the Excluded Amount

Mr. Coscia cites to PJM’s own words, and that of its expert witnesses who 
supported the introduction of RPM in the first place, showing that the IRAS 
Proposal is inconsistent with their statements of sound market design at the time.  
He explains:  
Consumers may pay lower Reliability Pricing Model charges in the 
near term, but that reduction results from buying less capacity, not 
from a reduction in the resources needed to serve the load or in the 
cost of providing them. PJM made the connection between reserve 
levels and consumer costs when it originally proposed the model 
more than twenty years ago. It told the Commission that recognizing 
value in capacity above the reserve margin dampens volatility and 
allows “investors to make reasonable predictions of revenue 
streams,” which “reduces reserve and capacity price volatility and 
consequently the return required by investors resulting in savings in 
consumer costs.” PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket Nos. ER05-
1410-000 and EL05-148-000, Transmittal at 24 (Aug. 31, 2005). PJM 
added that “additional reserves due to the VRR curve result in lower 
capacity and energy costs to consumers,” and that “[e]xcess reserves 
also further reduce the probability of loss of load and discourage 
withholding by suppliers to increase profits.” Id. at 24-25. It supported 
that with a table showing capacity cost falling as the reserve level 
cleared higher, and explained that the capacity savings “will be 
augmented by energy cost savings” because, as both Mr. Ott and 
Professor Hobbs explained, “the commitment of capacity at a higher 
reserve level will tend to decrease energy market prices.” Id. at 74 
(citing Ott Affidavit at 23-26). Reducing the reserves procured, as this 
filing proposes, should be expected to have the opposite result across 
each of those measures: a lower capacity charge, and higher energy

16 
costs, higher scarcity costs, and a higher probability of loss of load. 
The filing does not analyze that trade.34 
The IRAS Proposal would impose a market construct that is contrary to 
decades of well-established precedents providing that a just and reasonable 
market design must send appropriate price signals to encourage resource 
investment.35  Under applicable law, the Commission cannot depart from such 
well-established precedent without providing reasoned analysis justifying such 
departure,36 but PJM has utterly failed to provide the analysis the Commission 
would need to rely on.

“symmetrical, one-for-one addition” and yields “an effectively price-neutral

constructed, so the three points defining the downward-sloping portion are located at a 
smaller quantity: the Curve moves left and its sloped segments steepen. Reliability 
Backstop Procurement capacity offering at $0/MW-day separately moves supply right. 
Either change can reduce the clearing price where the auction clears on a price-responsive 
segment of the Demand Curve. 
10. My principal conclusion. The proposal separates the load PJM plans to serve from the 
capacity the Reliability Pricing Model procures to serve it. PJM designed that model to 
deliver, on average over an asset’s life, the net cost of new entry — the revenue a resource 
requires beyond what the energy and ancillary services markets provide. In 2005 PJM told 
the Commission the problem it sought to solve was that “net revenue to generators from all 
sources . . . has been insufficient to cover the cost of investment in the most efficient 
marginal capacity unit.” Id. at 7. The filing makes no showing that the price its design 
produces will deliver that revenue. 
11. Planning and procurement diverge. From 2028/2029 through 2032/2033, peak load net 
of load in an FRR Service Area grows 31,026 MW while the Reliability Requirement net of 
the Excluded Amount changes by 584 UCAP MW. These are not equivalent reliability 
measures, but their divergence shows that the procurement target no longer moves 
proportionately with the load PJM must plan to serve. Excluding load of that magnitude 
from the Demand Curve, year after year, bears directly on the premise of the construct. ¶ 
64. 
12. Investor perspective. I evaluate the proposal from the perspective of an investor 
deciding whether to build, finance or retain capacity in PJM. Entry and retention are 
connected over the life of an asset: every new resource becomes an existing resource, and 
both are required to maintain reliability. The results are scenarios, not forecasts, and 
Appendix A states the model and assumptions. 
13. The exclusion is large enough to matter. The 2028/2029 auction cleared 5,380 MW to 
the left of Point 1, the first of the three points from which the Demand Curve is constructed 
and the quantity at which the Curve reaches its maximum price. For 2029/2030 the 
modeled Excluded Amount closes all but approximately 290 MW of that distance. The 
auction therefore remains on the flat segment in the base case, and the collar 
independently controls that year’s result. The exclusion nevertheless makes the outcome 
sensitive to a small change in supply, and positions later auctions to clear on the reduced 
Curve once the collar expires. PJM offers no forecast of what this does to reliability, in 
terms either of retaining the current rate of new investment or of stemming recent 
retirements. ¶¶ 27–35. 
14. Modeled effect on clearing prices. The Excluded Amount does not change the supply 
available; it changes the Demand Curve against which that supply is offered. Holding the

4 
 
modeled supply path constant and changing only the Demand Curve, the modeled clearing 
price first falls below the most recently posted Net Cost of New Entry in 2030/2031, the 
first Delivery Year after the collar expires. ¶¶ 38–40. 
15. Consequences for entry and retention. Numerous price paths in the scenarios examined 
produce clearing prices below the most recently posted Net Cost of New Entry, and on 
several of them the shortfall persists across successive Delivery Years. PJM identified the 
consequence of revenues below that level in its 2005 filing: a spike in announced 
retirements of units that “nonetheless are needed for reliability,” and a warning that 
“generator revenues in PJM may not be adequate to sustain the investments needed to 
maintain reliability in all parts of the PJM region.” Id. at 6. A sustained price below that 
benchmark may weaken the signal for new entry and, depending on resource-specific 
going-forward costs, may also affect retention. ¶¶ 41–45, 63. 
16. Matched Bring Your Own New Capacity. PJM’s one-for-one rationale substantially holds 
where the supporting capacity is additional to projected additions, arrives with the load, 
and is deliverable to the relevant location. The Tariff permits configurations in which those 
conditions may not hold: the capacity may already be among the projected additions, may 
precede the load under section VII(h), or may sit outside a constrained Locational 
Deliverability Area in which the load remains excluded. The filing does not quantify those 
alternatives. ¶¶ 53–57. 
17. The reduction is not conditioned. The Fixed Resource Requirement Alternative, the Peak 
Shaving Adjustment and Price Responsive Demand each condition a reduction in the 
procurement target on a defined commitment, and Price Responsive Demand on a price 
stated in advance. The Excluded Amount is triggered by the appearance of load in a 
forecast. Unlike those mechanisms, the Excluded Amount is not conditioned on a specified 
commitment or performance requirement. ¶¶ 96-102, 134-135. 
18. The cumulative effect. If the filing is accepted, PJM will construct the 2029/2030 
Demand Curve using the reduced procurement base. The reduction will recur as qualifying 
load enters the forecast and will apply whether or not PJM ultimately calls an Interim 
Resource Adequacy Service event. Under the scenarios examined, the immediate effect is a 
smaller procurement target and increased sensitivity to the location of supply relative to 
Point 1; after the collar expires, several modeled paths produce materially lower clearing 
prices than the most recent Net Cost of New Entry calculation published by PJM. ¶¶ 64-68. 
19. The long-term effect. Load that is on the system and requires generation to serve it 
would be excluded from the Demand Curve. That is a departure from the premise of the 
construct, and if approved the filing would make the departure part of the ordinary 
operation of the Reliability Pricing Model rather than a one-time accommodation. PJM 
proposes no end date for the program. Where the Region is not short for three consecutive 
Delivery Years the program becomes dormant, but the Large Load Registry is retained and 
the exclusion re-emerges on a reset load vintage if shortfall conditions return. As additional 
qualifying load enters the forecast the Excluded Amount recurs and grows, and the filed 
Tariff does not state when previously excluded load returns to the procurement base. The

5 
 
result is a bifurcated capacity market: load inside the Demand Curve, against which PJM 
procures capacity, and load outside it, which PJM plans and operates the system to serve 
but does not buy against. A market in which a substantial and growing share of load sits 
outside the mechanism designed to price reliability weakens the connection between the 
system PJM plans to operate and the capacity the model procures, with corresponding 
consequences for entry, retention and resource adequacy. ¶¶ 64-68. 
20. Five matters warrant Commission attention: whether procurement against a reduced 
load base satisfies the same reliability criterion used to derive the planning parameters; 
whether the proposed mechanisms provide an equivalent accredited or binding substitute 
in every permitted configuration; whether the modeled price path remains adequate to 
support entry and retention; whether the differing treatment of other demand-side 
procurement reductions is justified; and whether the proposed compensation benchmark 
measures the service New Large Load provides. ¶¶ 146-151.

How I approached the question 
21. I evaluate how the proposal affects decisions to commit, retain or withdraw capital in 
PJM capacity. A resource that cannot expect to cover its going-forward costs may deactivate 
or leave the Region, and that decision responds to the same signal as a decision to build. 
Price is the mechanism through which a reduced procurement quantity reaches those 
decisions. New entry and retention are not separate market-design questions. Every new 
resource becomes an existing resource, and PJM must provide a sufficient and durable 
investment signal throughout the asset’s operating life. The Reliability Pricing Model was 
designed to deliver, on average over that life, the net cost of new entry: the revenue a 
resource requires beyond what the energy and ancillary services markets provide. That 
shortfall is what the capacity market exists to supply. A capacity market that lowers the 
revenue a resource can expect affects both the decision to build and the decision to keep 
operating, and resource adequacy depends on both. 
22. The mechanism works through the auction’s demand curve. PJM decides in advance 
how much capacity it will buy at each price, and that schedule is the Variable Resource 
Requirement Curve. The filing would subtract the Excluded Amount from the quantity on 
which that Curve is built, so PJM would buy less capacity at every price, while continuing to 
count the same load when it calculates how much capacity the Region needs to serve its 
load reliably. Separately, capacity procured through the Reliability Backstop Procurement 
is required to participate in the auction as a price taker at $0/MW-day, which adds supply 
that clears regardless of price. Buying less and adding supply that always clears both push 
the clearing price down. Neither does so while the auction clears on the flat portion of the 
Curve; once it clears on a sloped portion, both do.

and the prices run from the Point 1 price down to zero at Point 3. The Excluded Amount is 
subtracted inside the bracket, before the percentages are applied.

Your Own New Capacity coverage, and the allocation of RBP UCAP MW. None of those 
inputs will be known when an investor commits capital. An investor financing a long-lived 
generating asset would reflect the resulting range of potential capacity revenues in its 
required return, in financing terms, or in both. That is the uncertainty PJM said the 
Reliability Pricing Model would remove: in 2005 PJM told the Commission that recognizing 
capacity value above the reserve margin would dampen volatility, “making estimates of 
future prices more reliable and allowing investors to make reasonable predictions of 
revenue streams,” and would thereby “reduce[] . . . the return required by investors 
resulting in savings in consumer costs.” Id. at 24. 
63. The resource-adequacy effect reaches both entry and retention. A sustained price 
below the most recently posted Net Cost of New Entry benchmark weakens the signal for 
new investment. Lower expected capacity revenues may also affect retention, where an 
existing resource’s expected market revenues no longer cover its going-forward costs. 
Measured against the Reliability Requirement before the exclusion, the modeled market is 
short in every Delivery Year examined, and Appendix A.5 shows the shortfall widening 
across the period. New generation becomes existing generation, so the same market design 
reaches a resource first as a new entrant and later as an existing unit: capacity supporting a 
Bring Your Own New Capacity arrangement offers as a price taker for ten Delivery Years 
and then competes as merchant capacity, and backstop capacity does so for fifteen. The 
modeled price reduction is therefore not merely a redistribution of capacity-market 
revenues between sellers and buyers. It is the means by which the reduced procurement 
target reaches decisions to build, finance, retain or retire the resources PJM continues to 
rely on to serve the full load forecast.

Comparison of the procurement reductions 
96. PJM has established several ways to reduce the quantity of capacity it procures, and 
each of them requires something in return. The Fixed Resource Requirement Alternative, 
the Peak Shaving Adjustment and Price Responsive Demand each condition the reduction 
on a defined commitment or performance condition. The Excluded Amounts do not. 
Whether the exclusion is an appropriate continuing adjustment to the procurement base, 
rather than one more demand-side mechanism, turns on that difference. 
97. The Excluded Amounts operate by formula. As Appendix B explains, New Large Load 
above the 2028/2029 baseline holding neither Bring Your Own New Capacity nor Allocated

follows.

98. The Fixed Resource Requirement Alternative. An FRR Entity removes its load from the 
Reliability Pricing Model entirely, and must designate Capacity Resources in a quantity no 
less than the Forecast Pool Requirement multiplied by its allocated share of the 
Preliminary Zonal Peak Load Forecast. RAA, Schedule 8.1, section D.2. The plan must be 
approved, must run for a multi-year term, and must comprise only Capacity Performance 
Resources and Seasonal Capacity Performance Resources. Id. sections C.1, D.1.1. Deficiency 
is charged at the Point 1 price of the Variable Resource Requirement Curve. Id. section F.2. 
For the 2028/2029 Delivery Year the FRR reduction was 10,863.8 UCAP MW, subtracted on 
the same worksheet line as the Excluded Amounts would be. See Appendix A.2, paragraph 
A15.

compliance with Attachment DD-2, and exclusivity: “[a]ny End-Use Customer identified in

VII. CONCLUSION 
141. Interim Resource Adequacy Service addresses a real operational problem. PJM needs 
a means of protecting reliability if forecast New Large Load does not materialize as 
expected or cannot be served during stressed conditions. That objective does not resolve 
the market-design question examined in this affidavit: whether PJM may remove that load 
from the quantity it procures while continuing to include it in the studies that set the 
planning parameters and without identifying a corresponding adjustment to the capacity 
obligations allocated to Load Serving Entities. 
142. The price effect follows from the auction mechanics. The Excluded Amount shifts the 
Curve left and steepens its sloped segments; backstop capacity offered at $0/MW-day shifts 
supply right. Neither moves the price while the intersection stays on the horizontal

35 
 
segment. Once it reaches a sloped segment, both do. The 2029/2030 Excluded Amount 
alone brings supply within 290 MW of that point. 
143. Under the full-proxy scenario described in paragraph 42, the exclusion reduces the 
capacity revenue supporting both new investment and continued operation by 
approximately $127,276 per UCAP MW-year in 2030/2031, and the price falls below the 
most recently posted Net Cost of New Entry from that Delivery Year forward. Over the 
same period the procurement quantity ceases to track the load PJM must plan and operate 
the system to serve: peak load net of load in an FRR Service Area grows 31,026 MW while 
the Reliability Requirement net of the Excluded Amount moves 584 UCAP MW. 
144. The numerical results are scenarios rather than forecasts. They show the direction 
and range of the price effect under the stated assumptions concerning the New Large Load 
proxy, backstop participation, supply additions, Bring Your Own New Capacity, Allocated 
RBP UCAP MW, and the offer curve. PJM’s filing does not identify the threshold at which the 
exclusion begins to affect price, provide a sensitivity around the Excluded Amount, or 
evaluate the exclusion together with zero-priced backstop supply available in the same 
auctions. 
145. My analysis complements and extends the timing concern Dr. Shanker raises in the 
Constellation limited protest. He explains how backstop supply can enter the auction at 
zero before the associated load materializes. This affidavit addresses the demand side of 
that interaction. To the extent related RBP capacity is not allocated to the same load under 
Attachment DD-4, section IX, the Excluded Amount removes forecast load from the Curve 
while that capacity remains in the supply stack. The two mechanisms then operate on 
opposite sides of the same auction and press the clearing price in the same direction. 
146. Five unresolved features of the proposed design warrant Commission attention. 
147. PJM states in its 2028/2029 auction report that a price cap below the established 
Curve “can reduce the amount of investment, and therefore supply” in the Region. It ties 
market effectiveness to durability and identifies “backstop procurement mandates and 
price cap proposals” among the interventions that lead investors to discount the revenue 
stream. In the backstop proceeding, PJM proposes a maximum willingness to pay of 
$555/MW-day for capacity it will then require to offer into RPM at $0/MW-day. The filing 
does not reconcile the resulting reduction in the procurement quantity and potential 
clearing-price effect with the durable price signal PJM identifies as necessary. 
148. The filing does not test the resulting price against Net Cost of New Entry. That figure is 
PJM’s own estimate of the cost of bringing a new reference resource to the system, and the 
price coordinates of the Variable Resource Requirement Curve are derived from it. PJM 
proposes to modify the Curve without showing whether the prices it would produce 
remain adequate measured against the benchmark on which the Curve itself is built. 
149. PJM uses New Large Load in the load shapes from which it determines the Installed 
Reserve Margin, ELCC Class Ratings and Forecast Pool Requirement, but removes the 
Excluded Amount from the procurement quantity. The filing identifies no corresponding

36 
 
removal from the Obligation Peak Load used to allocate capacity obligations. See 
paragraphs 69 to 93. It therefore does not explain whether a conversion factor derived 
from the full load forecast remains appropriate when applied to a procurement quantity 
net of that load, or why load that continues to carry a capacity obligation should be 
removed from the quantity procured against it. 
150. The Fixed Resource Requirement Alternative, Peak Shaving Adjustment and Price 
Responsive Demand condition reductions in the procurement target on defined 
commitments or performance terms. Price Responsive Demand also conditions the 
reduction on a price stated by the provider in advance. See paragraphs 95 to 106. Interim 
Resource Adequacy Service, by contrast, reduces the procurement target when load enters 
the forecast without requiring a comparable binding commitment. The filing does not 
explain this difference. 
151. Section X(a) sets the Interim Resource Adequacy Service rate at 50 percent of a charge 
benchmarked to one year of Net Cost of New Entry and applied to capacity resources with 
capacity commitments. An Interim Resource Adequacy Service provider has no capacity 
commitment, receives no capacity-market payment for the service obligation, pays a 
Locational Reliability Charge through its Load Serving Entity, and is curtailed before the 
capacity-market participants whose performance charge supplies the benchmark. See 
paragraphs 113 to 136. An Eligible New Large Load may also elect a rate of zero. PJM relies 
principally on the Commission’s acceptance of related penalty and compensation 
constructs but does not explain why those constructs support compensation for an Interim 
Resource Adequacy Service provider with materially different obligations and economics. 
152. Interim Resource Adequacy Service may prove a useful operational backstop. The 
present record, however, does not establish an equivalence between the reduction in the 
quantity PJM procures and any accredited or binding commitment substituting for the 
capacity no longer bought. Until that equivalence is shown, the procurement reduction 
rests on the appearance of load in a forecast rather than on a resource-adequacy 
commitment the Tariff can enforce. I recommend that the Commission require PJM to 
resolve these matters before the exclusion first operates in the 2029/2030 Base Residual 
Auction.

APPENDIX B — ADDITIONAL IMPLEMENTATION ISSUE: 
ATTACHMENT DD-4, SECTION IV(b) 
B1. Attachment DD-4, section IV(b) governs the amount of Eligible New Large Load that 
must be available to provide Interim Resource Adequacy Service, determined after the 
Third Incremental Auction for each Delivery Year. It does not determine the amount 
removed from the auction procurement quantity. That reduction is made by the Excluded 
Amounts definitions and applied in Attachment DD, section 5.10(a). 
B2. The provision does not express its calculation unambiguously. Two features leave the 
formula unclear. 
B3. The placement of the divisor. In subsections (i) and (ii) the bracket encloses a 
comparison — capacity “is less than” the requirement — the division by the Pool-wide 
Accredited UCAP Factor follows the bracket, and a clause then measures the result against 
the Eligible New Large Load Amounts. In subsection (iii) the bracket encloses “equals or 
exceeds,” the division again follows a completed comparison, and nothing follows it. A 
comparison yields no quantity that can be divided. At least three readings are available: the 
divisor applies to the difference between the two quantities, to the requirement alone, or to 
nothing at all in subsection (iii). 
B4. The units on each side, and the factor used. Section V(b) converts Bring Your Own New 
Capacity and Allocated RBP UCAP MW to load by dividing by the Forecast Pool 
Requirement, and both Excluded Amounts definitions convert load to capacity “by using 
the Forecast Pool Requirement.” Section IV(b) instead applies the Pool-wide Accredited 
UCAP Factor, and measures the result against the Eligible New Large Load Amounts, which 
section V(b) defines as registered peak load less an offset — a quantity denominated in 
load. The Commission has described the Forecast Pool Requirement as reflecting “PJM’s 
installed capacity requirement in Unforced Capacity (UCAP) terms,” and as applied to a 
Demand Resource’s Nominated Value to yield unforced capacity. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 
186 FERC ¶ 61,080 at PP 2, 9 (2024). The Forecast Pool Requirement converts load to 
capacity; the Pool-wide Accredited UCAP Factor converts installed capacity to unforced 
capacity. 
B5. The Reliability Requirement is also unqualified. Section IV(b) refers to “the PJM Region 
Reliability Requirement determined prior to the Third Incremental Auction” without 
stating whether that quantity is gross or net of the Excluded Amounts, and without stating 
whether the comparison is made on a regional basis or net of the obligations of FRR 
Entities. Attachment DD, section 5.4(c)(2)(i) states a comparison of the same shape — the 
updated Reliability Requirement against total capacity committed — and there qualifies 
the requirement as “inclusive of any adjustments associated with Excluded RTO New Large 
Load Amounts or Excluded LDA New Large Load Amounts.” 
B6. PJM should state the calculation and its units expressly on the tariff sheets: what 
quantity the Pool-wide Accredited UCAP Factor operates on; the units on each side of the 
comparison; why that factor rather than the Forecast Pool Requirement; whether the

57 
 
Reliability Requirement is gross or net of the Excluded Amounts; and whether the 
comparison is regional or adjusted for FRR.

Years meet the requirements of section IV(b)(iii). The definition redefines New Large Load 
prospectively. Whether load already registered and excluded ceases to be excluded on the
